items.title: Cognition Ships SWE-2.1: Coding Scores Nearly Double, Plus a 10x Ultrafast Variant
items.summary: On Nov 24 Cognition released SWE-2.1, a major upgrade to the model behind Devin, again trained purely with reinforcement learning on Kimi K3. Cognition reports Terminal-Bench 4.1 at 50.0 versus 24.2 for SWE-2, FrontierCode 2.0 at 41.3 versus 24.1, ProgramBench at 44.0 versus 17.0, and SWE Marathon v1.2 at 54.9 versus 32.5. The company attributes the gains to training across short- and long-horizon workflows lasting minutes to hours; ExploitGym solve rates reportedly improve log-linearly with rollout time. Cyber capability jumped too: 80% on ExploitBench and 27.3% flag capture on ExploitGym. Two variants ship alongside it: SWE-2.1 Ultrafast, served with Cerebras at about 600 tokens/s versus 60 for the standard model, and SWE-2.1 Cyber with looser safeguards for Devin Security scans. A canary evaluation designed to detect sandbox escapes alerted researchers four times during training. All numbers are Cognition's own, measured in its own harness; no independent evaluation exists yet.
items.impact: Two signals matter more than the headline scores. First, long autonomous run time is now an explicit training target, so teams should re-test coding agents on multi-hour tasks rather than single-file fixes. Second, shipping a deliberately less restricted Cyber variant means the same lab is selling both offensive capability and defence tooling, which will draw safety scrutiny. For buyers, the 10x speed tier is aimed at live incident response, where inference latency itself becomes a cost.

items.title: Delegent: Local Small Models Cut Frontier Coding Cost by 67% Without Losing Tasks
items.summary: A preprint submitted Nov 24 (arXiv:2611.33098) by Lingwei Gu and Jimmy Lin introduces Delegent, a harness built on Claude Code in which a frontier model always leads the task while a local small model handles focused legwork: investigating code, running tests and searching a corpus. Unlike cascades or routers that pick one model for the whole task, no router or model is trained, so either component can be swapped. With GPT-6.1 Sol at high reasoning effort as the lead and Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 as the helper, frontier cost fell 67% on DeepSWE and 59% across 694 agentic-search questions, with the same number of tasks solved. A 2B laptop-class model (MiniCPM5-2B) cut coding cost by 66%. The authors note that a short instruction reserving main coding work for the frontier model accounts for most of the saving and prevents the 2B model from losing tasks. A repository is listed, but was not public as of Nov 25.
items.impact: This is a clean, reproducible version of the practical rule 'use the frontier model to think and a local model to grep'. It targets the real cost driver in long agent runs: re-reading an ever-growing context at frontier prices. Two caveats: the savings cover frontier API spend only, not the local GPU or its operation, and results are benchmark-specific. Treat this as a candidate for narrow, summarisable subtasks, not a reason to delegate refactors that need whole-repo reasoning.

items.title: Ant Ling Open-Sources Ling-3.2-air: A 124B Multimodal MoE Built for Repository Work
items.summary: Ant Group's Ling team released and open-sourced Ling-3.2-air on Nov 24 under an MIT license, with weights on Hugging Face and ModelScope. It keeps the native multimodal architecture of Ling-3.0-flash-VL, accepting text, images and video, with 124B total parameters and 5.5B activated per token, roughly 22% of the size of the earlier Ling-3.2-flash flagship. Against its predecessor, SWE-bench Pro rose from 26.40 to 58.28, Terminal-Bench 4.0 from 0 to 27.0, AutomationBench-AA from 15.7% to 61%, and SkillsBench from 42.91 to 67.82; HLE went from 21.96 to 31.42. The gap to frontier models remains clear on long professional workflows: on Harvey LAB-AA v1.1 the model satisfied 87.7% of individual criteria but fully passed only 8.3% of tasks, dropping to 0.8% once major factual hallucinations were checked.
items.impact: An open-weight, permissively licensed model that nearly doubled its repository-level software-engineering score is a useful option for teams that must keep code and prompts inside their own infrastructure. The more instructive number is the legal benchmark: passing most sub-criteria is not the same as completing a task, so evaluate open models on end-to-end pass rates for your own workflows.

items.title: XPeng Unveils Turing Embodied Architecture; IRON Humanoid Set for Mass Production in January
items.summary: At its eighth Technology Day in Guangzhou on Nov 25, XPeng announced the Turing embodied-intelligence architecture, a shared stack for cars, robotaxis and humanoids. It layers System 2 for goal reasoning and planning, System 1 for action policy and System 0 for real-time control; the second-generation VLA model reached version 6.4.0 with agent-style closed-loop training, 10-12x faster training, recursive self-evolution and self-distillation so the policy can run on smaller compute budgets. The IRON humanoid gave a bilingual speech and took live questions without teleoperation. Hardware: 76 degrees of freedom, more than 1,500 tactile contact points, over 80% tactile coverage in core areas, and three in-house Turing chips delivering about 2,250 TOPS on device. XPeng says hardware mass production starts January 2027, with store assistant trials in Q1, a public launch in Q2 and a robot application ecosystem platform. All figures and timelines are company-stated.
items.impact: The interesting bet is architectural reuse: one S2/S1/S0 foundation claimed to serve both vehicles and a humanoid, with VLA self-distillation bridging high- and low-compute hardware. That could shorten robot development if it holds. Treat the January mass-production date and onstage autonomy as milestones to verify, not evidence of deployed reliability.

items.title: Zhejiang Humanoid Ships SPIRE 2.0, Aligning Data, Representation, Policy and Skills for Long Tasks
items.source: Leiphone / Zhejiang Humanoid Robot Innovation Center
items.summary: Announced Nov 25 and reported Nov 26, SPIRE 2.0 is an update to Zhejiang Humanoid's full-chain embodied system built around task alignment. NaviDataset now holds more than 220,000 finely annotated real-robot dexterous-operation trajectories and over 810,000 frames of spatial perception data across automotive manufacturing, garment production, warehousing and lab work. NaviRepresentation aligns tasks with modalities, time/space, and body/environment; NaviPolicy combines NaviVLA and NaviVLN with fundamental skills; NaviAssistant coordinates multiple models and re-plans when a step fails; NaviSkillLib stores reusable skills. Company-reported results: 1/5 of the training data of comparable methods for equivalent navigation performance, +9% simulated success and +25% success on unseen real tasks versus a VLA baseline, and on the NAVIAI i2 platform 66.1% better tracking accuracy with 11.5% shorter traversal time. In garment production, fabric sorting reaches 98%, pocket attachment takes 35 seconds per piece and system success exceeds 90%; bin picking reports over 90% first-grasp success.
items.impact: This is a concrete answer to a problem pure model scaling does not solve: how to keep a multi-step industrial task aligned when objects, contact conditions and bodies change. The emphasis on a reusable skill library and multi-model coordination mirrors the agent-harness pattern in software. All numbers are the centre's own, without independent replication, and the published evidence is production claims rather than a public benchmark.
